brief.text: Google let staff spend funded hours on side projects. Judged one by one, Amit Varma said, they look like a distraction; as a culture, they are “massively plus EV”. {022-C03}

brief.head: Great people volunteer

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on three audacious firms
lead.head: Giant leaps for firmkind
body: Ajay Shah once claimed expertise in sixteen things, and Amit Varma, reporting that “hashtags have been formed”, demanded at least one more. Shah’s answer was firms. {022-J01}

Firms normally grow by economies of scale, doing more of what they know, or by economies of scope, moving into adjacencies. Three firms, Shah said, did not fit any standard conception of how firms grow.
Sun Microsystems, Google and Amazon did neither. “It was not economies of scale, it was not really economies of scope, and it was jumping to something way more complicated,” Shah said. {022-C01}
## Three jumps
In the late 1980s, Sun assembled workstations from Motorola CPUs and off-the-shelf parts. When Motorola hit a wall, Sun began designing its own CPUs, and invented a new architecture, SPARC. {022-S01}

Google started as a search engine and came to see itself as an infrastructure company. Then it took on Android, which Andy Rubin brought to it. An operating system, Shah said, is the most complex piece of software. {022-S02}

Amazon, by his account doing “the dullest thing in the world” as an online bookshop, began renting out the computers it had bought for the Christmas rush, and effectively invented cloud computing. {022-S03}
So a computer maker, a search company and a bookshop each jumped, in Shah’s words, into “the world’s most complex thing”.
## The nerve to jump
What made the leaps possible? Shah listed internal cash flows and the love of financial markets, insiders asking hard questions about threats, and leaders with deep engineering credibility.

At Sun, he said, Bill Joy and Andreas Bechtolsheim were so respected that essentially anybody in the world would have joined them. Google, in his telling, inherited a Unix culture that ran from Sun through Netscape.

“Execution is commoditized,” Shah said. Mainstream Indian firm culture, he argued, obsesses over it and over obedient people, and is weak in strategic thinking: part of what makes India a poor country.
He also checked himself for survivorship bias, asking whether many firms had leapt and a few landed by dumb luck. Having watched these three for years, he still thinks they were special.
## Leaps of imagination
Varma objected to “just a bookshop”. Imagining a bookshop on the internet, he said, was itself a spectacular leap. For him, such leaps owe more to creative storytelling than to linear business logic.
A good business leader can be made with an MBA, execution and incentives, he said. A great one needs to be an artist, able to tell a new story about what the firm really is.

His examples included the valuation expert Aswath Damodaran, who changed his mind about Uber after Bill Gurley told him he had the wrong story, and Netflix, which moved to streaming at the peak of its DVD business.
The recommendations turned to the craft behind such leaps. Shah chose Tracy Kidder’s *The Soul of a New Machine*, his first glimpse, when young, of engineering done with all your heart and soul.

Varma read from Rick Rubin’s *The Creative Act*: turning an idea into reality can make it seem smaller. Shah said he sees the opposite, with work becoming more beautiful at every pass. “So I always love my babies much better at the end than at the beginning,” he said.
“Because young babies are a pain,” Varma replied.

second.label: The Uber valuation
second.head: Wrong story, wrong price
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Aswath Damodaran changed his mind about Uber, publicly
body: Around 2014, the valuation expert Aswath Damodaran wrote a sceptical post on Uber. His story, Amit Varma said, was that Uber was in the taxi and car-service business, a market of $100 billion, of which it would get at most 10 per cent. {#tam}
Bill Gurley, a legendary investor and an early backer of Uber, replied that Damodaran had the wrong story. Uber was out to replace car ownership, a far bigger market. {022-R05}

Damodaran agreed in public that Gurley was right, which Varma held up as a model of intellectual honesty. {022-S04} He redid his valuation: as Varma remembers it, from about $5 billion to about $28 billion. {#valuation}

quote.text: When you’re doing something so new, you cannot look at what exists.

second.caption: the Uber valuation

third.head: Not a Kodak moment
body: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD rental business. In 2007 it shipped its billionth DVD; the film, Amit Varma noted for the trivia-minded, was *Babel*. {#billionth}
At that point it seemed to have cornered the market. “But they could have made the same mistake that Kodak made with film,” Varma said, “and refuse to accept that the world was changing.” {022-S05}

Instead, under Reed Hastings, it accepted the change and started a streaming service. Varma thinks it began by making the third season of *Breaking Bad* big, then went on to commission *House of Cards*.
For Varma, Netflix shows what lifts a business leader from good to great: the ability to tell a new story about the firm. {022-C09}
third.caption: Netflix and Kodak

p2.title: The leap years
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s three firms that jumped, and Amit Varma on the storytelling behind the jump

sections.label: The first leap
sections.head: Sun, out of Motorola’s shadow
sections.caption: Sun’s leap into CPUs
body: In the late 1980s, Ajay Shah said, Sun Microsystems made workstations from off-the-shelf parts, with CPUs bought from Motorola. Its real innovation was the operating system, a variant of BSD Unix from UC Berkeley brought in by its co-founder Bill Joy.

Then Motorola got stuck and could not make its CPUs faster, and Sun’s computers stalled with them. Meanwhile labs at Stanford and Berkeley were brewing a controversial idea, reduced instruction set computing: make the CPU very simple, and it goes fast.
Sun put two and two together and leapt into making CPUs. {022-S01} It invented an architecture called SPARC, and for a run of about ten years it was successful and influential. {#sparc}
## Nerve and money

Amit Varma noted that, as Clayton Christensen points out in *The Innovator’s Dilemma*, big companies tend to get ossified, with disruption coming from small upstarts. {022-R07} So what, he asked, impressed Shah most?
“CPUs are truly hard,” Shah said. Sun also needed money, which meant internal cash flows and the love of financial markets. As he put it, “Wall Street tells Main Street what to do.” {022-J12}

It also had two revered engineers, Bill Joy and Andreas Bechtolsheim, who gave the firm the confidence that it could do anything. Varma had his own reason to admire Joy: “Who cannot like a guy with a name like that.”
~ Sun made a similar leap with Java, Shah noted, though nobody makes money from a programming language.

quote.text: A normal computer maker chose to jump into the world’s most complicated design and manufacturing problem, namely CPUs. And they pulled it off.

portraits.hint: American computer engineer, co-founder of Sun Microsystems

sections.label: The second leap
sections.head: Beyond the search box
sections.caption: Google’s engineering culture
body: Google began as a search engine built on PageRank, where, Ajay Shah noted, the “Page” is Larry Page, not a web page. Downloading and indexing the entire internet led it to see itself as an infrastructure company, one that knew how to handle more CPUs than anyone.

The normal next step was economies of scope: search for movies or music, or a search box for a company’s private data. Instead Google set out to organise the whole world’s information, and leapt into writing an operating system, Android. {#tagline}

Amit Varma pointed out that Larry Page and Sergey Brin started Google straight out of college, before corporate thinking could indoctrinate them. It funded employees’ side projects, which he called “massively plus EV” as a bet on culture. {022-C03}
## Above the API

Shah’s answer was aesthetics. Engineers see the difference between a clean design and a bad one, even when two products look the same from outside. A “shut up and get it done” culture creates bad products in the medium term and drives away the best people. {022-C04}
Routine work can be run with instructions and tyrannical bosses, he said. Creative work above the API, where people dream and strategise, cannot.
~ He recalled a line from Nachiket Mor: “People respond to incentives, great people volunteer.” {022-C06}

quote.text: So of course we need execution, but execution is commoditized. And you can get execution guys a dime a dozen.

portraits.hint: American computer scientist, co-founder of Google
American computer scientist, co-founder of Google

sections.label: The third leap
sections.head: Paise, PhDs and servers
sections.caption: Amazon’s leap into the cloud
body: Ajay Shah began his third story by deflating his subject. Amazon, he said, was a bookshop, a Flipkart, a Myntra, doing “the dullest thing in the world”: putting lots of SKUs on a screen and grinding out deliveries.
It was also, he said, “the biggest recruiter in the whole world of PhDs in economics”, hired to “con you out of 35 more paise for the shirt”. {022-J04}

Then it began renting out the computers it had bought for the Christmas rush, wrapped in an API. That meant building something as complex as an operating system, and Amazon effectively invented cloud computing. {022-S03}
## Just a bookshop?

Amit Varma objected. Imagining a bookshop on the internet, rather than an actual bookshop, was itself a spectacular leap, he said, and Jeff Bezos one of the great men of the last couple of decades. Shah restated the argument, that Flipkart and Myntra were me-toos while Amazon imagined e-commerce itself, and called it a fair point.

Shah also tested his own thesis. Perhaps many firms tried audacious leaps and a few succeeded by dumb luck. That, he said, is why the show will never do an episode on three great fund managers. {022-J05}
~ Having watched these three firms for many years, he still believes they were special, and he invited listeners to argue the point in the comments. {022-C07}

quote.text: You throw 10,000 darts, 10 are going to look great.

sections.label: The storyteller
sections.head: Once upon a valuation
sections.caption: telling a firm’s story
body: Leaps like these, Amit Varma argued, are more an act of creative storytelling than of linear business logic. When Google said it would organise the world’s information, that audacity mattered.
He drew on Aswath Damodaran’s *Narrative and Numbers*, which, he said, goes beyond valuation into what firms are about and the stories they tell themselves. {022-R03}

Damodaran had valued Uber as a taxi business. When Bill Gurley argued that Uber was out to replace car ownership, Damodaran agreed and redid his sums. Something truly new, Varma said, cannot be sized by what exists.
He showed a tweet by Aaron Levie: sizing a disruptor by the incumbent’s market “is like sizing the car industry of how many horses there were in 1910”. {022-C08}
## Coffee or real estate?

Ten years ago, Varma said, a food delivery market sized by calls to restaurants would have looked minuscule. Then delivery changed how nuclear families with two working partners live, and cloud kitchens came up serving home-like food.

Is Starbucks a coffee vendor, he asked, or in real estate, because people need a place to sit and work? Is Walmart a retailer, or leasing space to brands? Are tech giants monopolies, or rivals fighting for our attention?
~ Execution and incentives make a good leader, he said; a great one also has to be a storyteller. {022-C09}

quote.text: But to be great, I think you also have to be a little bit of a storyteller.

sections.label: The reccos
sections.head: First drafts, last loves
sections.caption: making peace with first drafts
body: Amit Varma recommended Rick Rubin’s *The Creative Act* to all businessmen: to succeed at anything, he said, you need imagination and must think like a creator. {022-R02}
He read Rubin’s line that turning an idea into reality can make it seem smaller. A first draft disappoints, Varma said, and a business plan meets trouble and pivots until the original idea is gone.

Ajay Shah said he sees it exactly the opposite way. His book with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, began as a dutiful primer and became, through page-by-page sessions in Pune, a creative project. {#pune}
“So it actually goes off as an exponential,” Shah said: a product starts workmanlike and becomes more beautiful as you go. {022-C10}
## Many roads to a page

Robert Lucas, Shah said, did ten complete rewrites; Paul Graham, Varma added, workshops each essay for a couple of months, while George Orwell banged out three or four brilliant columns a week. Varma bridged the two views with the show’s mantra, *kaator re bhaaji*: keep putting in the work, and magic can happen.
~ For the stuck, he offered Hemingway’s cure: write one true sentence, then one more, true meaning authentic to that moment. {022-C12}

quote.text: But the important thing is you have to put your bum on that chair and get the writing done.

side.boxText: Production in a market economy is organised in firms, Ajay Shah said, and India needs firms with the productivity and capabilities of those in advanced economies. He sees India’s journey as synonymous with building great firms. {#journey}

contQuote.text: The best engineers are there to build something beautiful. They’re not there to meet that KRA. They’re not there to dance to the tune of corporate HR.

p3.deck: A phone deal, a Christmas rush, a book and a hero’s ten rewrites

stories.start: and there is a sweet little story. There, the uh project Android
stories.end: today it is one of the most important operating systems of the whole world
stories.caption: Android’s late-evening call
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how Android found its way to Google
stories.head: Android phones home
body: Andy Rubin had been building Android, Ajay Shah said, nurturing it and building it, and it was not working too well. Phones of that age lacked the CPU power and battery life to do any meaningful calculations.
At some point Rubin ran out of steam. He was about to sell the project to a Canadian telecom company. {#canadian}

Then, in the version of the story Shah read in the press, Rubin reached out to Google late one evening. Tomorrow morning, he said, he was going to sign the term sheet. But he would love it if the project went to Google, and he would go with it.
“This project really belongs in Google, that Google has the culture, has the engineering capability, has the hunger to do justice to Android,” Shah recounted Rubin saying. {022-S02}
It was thrashed out over that evening. Google bought Rubin’s company, and turned a flaky early Android into one of the most important operating systems in the world.

Why Google? Shah traced an old Unix culture in Silicon Valley that coalesced at Sun and moved through Netscape to Google. Eric Schmidt had been chief scientist at Sun; Unix legends from Bell Labs, like Rob Pike, worked at Google.

~ For an engineer with the love of his life to place, Shah said, Google was the obvious home. And for Google it was a leap like Sun’s into CPUs: a search company writing the most complex software there is.
stories.why: A strong engineering culture works like a magnet: great engineers bring their best work to the firm they trust to do it justice. Execution can be bought, Shah said; great leaps of ideas are scarce. {022-C05}

stories.start: Okay, and my third story of this nature is Amazon.
stories.end: turn into one of the important computer science corporations of the world?
stories.caption: the Christmas servers
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Amazon’s idle computers
stories.head: Christmas comes but once a year
body: Before Christmas, Ajay Shah said, Amazon saw ridiculous surges of demand. Never wanting to turn away a customer, it sized its computers for the peak.

So for most of the year the equipment sat idle. Amazon was paying the cost of capital 365 days a year on machines really used for 10 or 15. {#capital} Then came the aha moment: package up that spare capacity, wrap it in an API and rent it out to other people. {#api}

That meant building something as complex as an operating system, which a Flipkart or a Myntra would flat out refuse, Shah said. Amazon did it, and effectively invented cloud computing, which it still dominates. {022-S03}
~ Shah still looks back in wonder, he said, that a bookshop turned into one of the important computer science corporations of the world.
stories.why: A cost headache, idle servers, became a world-changing business because Amazon did not let its self-image as an e-commerce shop limit what it attempted. A typical firm, in Shah’s telling, would have said “that’s not our capability”.

stories.start: when Kilkar and I started this book, our objectives are relatively modest
stories.end: I always love my babies much better at the end than at the beginning.
stories.caption: writing with Vijay Kelkar
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on writing a book with Vijay Kelkar
stories.head: The chore that came alive
body: When Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar started *In Service of the Republic*, the aim was modest: a primer carrying knowledge from public administration to economists, and from economics to public administrators. It was a chore, Shah said, done as a responsibility.
Around 20 chapters deep, he was not having fun. {#chapters}

Their method was to revise and revise. Then Shah would carry a physical hard copy to Pune, and the two would spend a half day or a full day walking through every page. {#pune} Twenty ideas would come up, and each innovation fed on the next until the chore became a creative project.
~ The language improves the same way, Shah said: on the first draft it is always bad, and around the 15th rewrite it becomes good. {#rewrite}

quote.text: So I always love my babies much better at the end than at the beginning.

stories.postscript: “Because young babies are a pain,” Amit Varma replied. {022-J07}

stories.start: So one of my hero is Robert Lucas, the economist who died recently.
stories.end: Then I finish with my hard working phase and then the joy starts.
stories.caption: Robert Lucas’s ten rewrites
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a master economist wrote
stories.head: Bin it and begin again
body: Robert Lucas, the economist who had died recently, is one of Ajay Shah’s heroes. Shah puts him in Milton Friedman’s league for the beauty of his writing, and spent a lot of time studying how both men wrote.
Then one day Lucas said that any article required ten complete rewrites: literally throwing a draft away and writing it all over again from scratch. {#lucas}
“And that was an eye opener for me,” Shah said, “and it helped me to make peace with the crappy stuff that I do at the early stages.” {022-S07}
~ All products start out bad, he said, and you have to shoe-leather them, making them better and better. When the sparks of life come in, the hard-working phase ends and the joy starts.
stories.why: A master’s early drafts are bad too, which frees the rest of us from despair. Amit Varma added that methods differ, from Paul Graham’s months of workshopping to George Orwell’s weekly columns, but the bum must meet the chair. {022-C11}
